## 2.1. Quality control

Approximately 10% of the samples were analyzed in duplicate, with the differences between duplicates being less than 15%; at least one reagent blank and a certified reference material were also included in each analysis batch.

Reference materials used were NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, MD, USA) 8436 -Durum Wheat Flour, NIST 1568a -Rice Flour, NIST 1547 -Peach Leaves, NIST 1570a -Spinach Leaves, and IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency, Vienna, Austria) 336 -Lichen. For most elements the relative standard deviation of duplicate analyses was less than 10%, with a few (Al, Mo, S, U) having RSD between 10 and 20%; elements with RSDs greater than 20% were those which approached the detection limit of the technique (Ca, V, Ba, Sb, Sm). The agreement between techniques was excellent. Recovery for all reference materials used (were within acceptable limits of /C6 15%.

In the laboratory, the rice samples were air dried, crushed, and sieved to 150 meshes. For total mercury (THg) analysis, rice samples were digested in a water bath (95 °C) with a fresh mixed acid of HNO3:H2SO4 (4:1, v/v) (Horvat et al., 1991) and determined by SnCl2 reduction, purge, gold trap, and cold vapor atomic /uniFB02 uorescence spectrometry (CVAFS) detection according to USEPA Method 1631 (USEPA, 1999).

For MeHg measurement, rice samples were digested using the KOH-methanol/solvent extraction technique (Liang et al., 1994, 1996) and measured by aqueous ethylation, purge, trap, and gas chromatography (GC) coupled with CVAFS detection according to USEPA Method 1630 (USEPA, 2001). Detail information of quality control is available in the Supporting information.

## 3.1.4. Mercury

The average mercury content of the white rice samples ranged from < 0.015 to < 0.085 mg/kg while the range for brown rice was < 0.024 to < 0.112 mg/kg. The mean values in white rice and brown rice were < 0.049 mg/kg and < 0.062 mg/kg respectively. Mercury has no known essentiality in humans and the toxic effects of mercury compounds and in particular methylmercury are well known.

Methylmercury poisoning through the ingestion of fish from industrially contaminated waters was the cause of mass poisoning in Minamata, Japan (Ekino et al., 2007). The symptoms of mercury poisoning range from the neurological to the renal, reproductive and cardiovascular systems and its effect on the nervous system of the developing fetus have been described (McDowell, 1992; Berry, 2008).

Using synchrotron X-ray /uniFB02 uorescence (XRF) and particle induced X-ray emission (PIXE) to map the locations of nutrients in the rice grain, Lombi et al. (2009) reported both Zn and Cu decreased in concentration from the pericarp to the interior of the endosperm, while K and Mn were localized in the aleurone/pericarp region. During the milling process, the embryo, pericarp and most of the aleurone layer are removed, leaving polished white rice. In rice grain, the /uniFB01 lial tissue (endosperm, germ, and aleurone) is isolated from the maternal tissue (pericarp, placenta, vascular tissue, chalaza, and nucellus) (Krishnan and Dayanandan, 2003). The ovular vascular trace, which is part of the maternal tissue, is the only source of nutrients for the developing grain (Krishnan and Dayanandan, 2003), and is considered a bottleneck for nutrient unloading (Lombi et al., 2009). It is possible organic nutrients, including MeHg, utilize membrane transport pathways into the grain more ef /uniFB01 ciently, which was reported in rice grain for organic dimethylarsinic acid (Carey et al., 2010; Lombi et al., 2009; Meharg et al., 2008) and for organic selenium species (Li et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2009).

Recent studies have highlighted that rice can accumulate relatively high levels of MeHg (174 ng·g -1 ) in mercury (Hg) mining areas in Guizhou Province, Southwestern China (Horvat et al., 2003; Qiu et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010a). Shi et al. (2005) also found the MeHg concentrations in rice samples produced in 15 provinces in China ranged from 1.9 to 10.5 ng·g -1 . Furthermore, rice, rather than /uniFB01 sh, is the main route of human MeHg exposure in Wanshan Hg mining area (Feng et al., 2008) and even in Guizhou Province in China (Zhang et al., 2010b). The bioavailability of Hg in rice is not known but adverse effects including neurobiological disruptions and increase of c-fos gene expression have been observed in rats feeding experiments with MeHg contaminated rice (Cheng et al., 2006; Ji et al., 2006). The probable daily intake (PDI) of MeHg from rice consumption indicated potential human health risk in Hg mining areas (Feng et al., 2008; Li et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2010b). The MeHg translocation and accumulation in rice plant (Meng et al., 2010, 2011) and the effects of mitigation methods and cultivar variations (Peng et al., 2012; Rothenberg et al., 2011) were observed.

Withrapideconomicgrowthinthelast 3 decades, China is considered as the largest anthropogenic source of Hg emission in the world (Pacyna et al., 2006). Its annual Hg emission reached 604.7 t in 2000, accounting for 28% of the global emissions (Pacyna et al., 2006). Coal combustion and non-ferrous metal smelting are the most important anthropogenic sources (Streets et al., 2005). The large Hg emissions have resulted in serious environmental Hg pollution in China (Feng, 2004; Jiang et al., 2006; Zhang and Wong, 2007). But there are no comprehensive studies regarding this environmental health problem to evaluate human Hg exposure and associated health effects.

Furthermore, Hg concentrations in soil are not evenly distributed over China; southern China has higher Hg concentrations than northern China (Zheng, 1994) as the Global Circum-Paci /uniFB01 c Hg Belt crosses southern China (Feng, 2004). Northern and southern China are divided by the Huai River-Qinling Mountains in geography, with big differences in climate (cold and dry in northern China; warm and rainy in southern China), geography, culture, language, and cuisine. Rice is the second largest produced crop in the world and China is the largest rice producer with 30.7% of the global production (UNCTAD, 2011).

Southern China is the main rice cultivation area accounting for 93% of national rice production in 2009 (NBS, 2010) and rice is the staple food for the population in this region. The relative high Hg background in the soil (Zheng, 1994) andfrequentrice intake indicate that the general population in southern China may be at risk of elevated exposure to MeHg.

The objective of this study was to evaluate human health risk through rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption in southern China and to calculate the relative contribution from rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption. It will provide an overview of human MeHg exposure and risk assessment and new understanding of MeHg exposure pathways in southern China.

## 2. Materials and methods

## 2.1. Sample collection

A total of 284 polished rice samples ( Oryza sativa L.) were collected in 2007 from markets in urban area or residents' house in rural area in 7 provinces in southern China, which include 4 coastal area: Guangdong ( n =47),

There are clear differences in the pattern of rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption between urban and rural population as a result of income difference (Supporting information Table S3). As incomes rise, diets improve: the city dweller consumes signi /uniFB01 cantly less grain and more meat, /uniFB01 sh, fruits and vegetables than the rural counterpart (NBS, 2010).

## 4.3. Potential health risk

Overall, the average PDI of MeHg from rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption was below the guidelines for public health concerns. However, the 95th percentile PDI of MeHg from rice consumption for rural population in Hunan exceeded the RfD of 0.1 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 for children and pregnant women established by the USEPA (1997), which indicated some subpopulations may be at potential risk of MeHg exposure.

Other high risk groups include residents in regions affected by point sources of Hg pollution.

For example, Zhang et al. (2010b) predicted that approximately 22,400 and 107,200 residents in Guizhou Hg mining areas were exposed to MeHg exceeding the JEFCA and USEPA guideline, respectively. Besides Hg mining areas, the population in the vicinity of hotspots of Hg pollution, such as amalgamation gold mining, chemical plant, metal smelting and coal combustion power plant, may be also at potential risk of MeHg exposure (Feng, 2004; Li et al., 2009).

The results of PDIs of MeHg from rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption (0.020 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 for urban population and 0.028 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 for rural population) were comparable with the previous report on MeHg exposure from /uniFB01 sh consumption in 12 provinces in China (0.006 μ g· kg -1 ·d -1 , Shang et al., 2010), US adult women (0.02 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 , Mahaffey et al., 2004), Korean population (0.03 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 , Lee et al., 2006), and Southeast Asia populations (0.027 -0.097 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 , Agusa et al., 2007), but were lower than that reported in Japanese populations with high /uniFB01 sh consumption (0.14 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 , Zhang et al., 2009). The results of this study con /uniFB01 rmed the low risk of human MeHg exposure through rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption in southern China, even serious environmental Hg pollution were found in China (Feng, 2004; Jiang et al., 2006; Zhang and Wong, 2007).

The low averages of hair THg concentrations (generally b 1 μ g/g) reported in /uniFB01 ve coastal sites (Shanghai, Ningbo, Dalian, Xiamen, and Zhoushan) in eastern China (Liu et al., 2008) also con /uniFB01 rmed our results in this study.

Because rice does not contain a lot of bene /uniFB01 cial micronutrients associated with /uniFB01 sh (e.g., n -3long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid, selenium, the essential amino acids, Li et al., 2010a, 2010b), the current Reference Doses of MeHg exposures from /uniFB01 sh consumption may underestimate the health effects of MeHg exposure from rice consumption. It is urgent and critical to setup the dose -response relationship of MeHg exposure from rice consumption and to reduce the health risk in southern China.

## 5. Conclusions

Theaveragelevels of THg and MeHg in the rice samples collected from southern China were generally low.

But 12.7% of the rice samples had THg concentration exceeding the national limit. The general populations in southern China had low risk of MeHg exposure through rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption. However, rice consumption is still the main route of MeHg exposure for rural population in southern China.

## 3.2.6. Magnesium

Magnesium concentrations in white rice ranged from 176 to 562 mg/kg, and 340 to 1450 mg/kg in brown rice.

The mean concentration found in white rice was 371 mg/kg and the mean in brown rice was 1205 mg/kg. Bulk rice had a value of 381 mg/kg and as such may not be an adequate source of dietary magnesium, but several types of Jamaican foods do contain significant levels of magnesium (Howe et al., 2005). Magnesium toxicity whether by dietary intake or parenteral administration is improbable as excessive magnesium is excreted (Rude, 1998). Magnesium

deficiency in animals and humans however, is well known and described in literature. Symptoms range from growth retardation, nausea, muscle weakness, tetany and this deficiency may affect cardiac function (McDowell, 1992). It was thought the typical westernized diet provided adequate magnesium; however a significant amount of the US population may be falling short of recommended intake amounts (Rude, 1998). This may suggest that a tendency toward deficiency is more likely than previously estimated. According to the NIH, a cup of cooked brown rice contains approximately 80 mg of magnesium, which would be about 20% of RDA.

## 3.2.7. Manganese

The manganese concentrations in white rice samples ranged from 5.02 to 17.1 mg/kg; the range for brown rice was 5.1943.5 mg/kg. The mean concentration of manganese in the white rice samples analyzed was 10.5 mg/kg and 26.5 mg/kg in brown rice samples, with Roland Black Japonica rice having the highest levels. Brown rice is known as a good source of manganese and several of the samples had manganese levels in excess of 30 mg/ kg. Manganese is essential to human beings. It can function as an enzyme activator for several enzymes and as a component of some metalloenzymes.

It is also important for bone growth, carbohydrate and lipid metabolism. Because of its ubiquity in foods, deficiency is unlikely in an adequate diet.
